usage: Guest to hotel front desk, polite and natural
반말 — only muttered to a friend you're traveling with, never to staff
More formal 격식 — at a nicer hotel or business trip
Softer opener that invites the clerk to take over
examples: 안녕하세요, 체크인할게요.
Hi, I'd like to check in.
The standard one-line opener at any front desk; the -ㄹ게요 ending makes your intention clear without sounding demanding
A: 어서 오세요. / B: 안녕하세요, 체크인할게요. 이름은 김민수예요.
A: Welcome. / B: Hi, I'd like to check in. The name is Kim Minsu.
Typical A/B exchange at arrival — give your name right after so the clerk can pull up the booking
지금 체크인할 수 있어요? 시간이 좀 이른데요.
Can I check in now? It's a bit early.
Real early-arrival situation — 체크인할게요 upgrades to a question only here because you're unsure the room is ready
nuance: 체크인할게요 is the guest's opener to hotel staff to start the check-in process. The -ㄹ게요 ending communicates your own confident intention ('I'll go ahead and check in') and is warm, polite, and perfectly calibrated for service situations — not a question, not a command. To go more formal use 체크인 부탁드립니다 or the crisper 체크인하겠습니다. The softer 체크인하려고 하는데요 trails off so the clerk takes the lead — choose -ㄹ게요 when you're ready and direct, -려고 하는데요 when you want them to guide you. With a travel companion you might say 체크인하자 ('let's check in'), but you would never drop 반말 with the desk clerk. English speakers often open with 체크인할 수 있어요? ('am I able to check in?'), which sounds as if you doubt it's possible; just state 체크인할게요. Also remember 체크인 is a noun and needs -하다, so the clipped 체크인요 sounds unfinished.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I will check in (as my intention)'. The -ㄹ게요 ending signals your own willful intention, not a permission-seeking question. It is the natural, polite opener a guest directs at front-desk staff to kick off the process — confident but not blunt.

Standard-polite (존댓말). Use this at any hotel, hostel, or guesthouse counter with staff you don't know. Upgrade to 체크인 부탁드립니다 or 체크인하겠습니다 at upscale or business hotels. Use 체크인하려고 하는데요 when you'd rather the staff lead the conversation.

체크인하려고 하는데요 ('I'm here to check in...') invites the clerk to take charge of the process; use it when you want to be guided. 체크인할게요 is you announcing what you are about to do, so it is the more assertive, direct opener. Neither is rude — they differ in who drives the interaction.

Formality scale: 체크인하겠습니다 (격식, formal—business hotels, written requests) → 체크인할게요 (standard polite) → 체크인하려고 하는데요 (deferential trailing form) → 체크인하자 (반말 proposal to a companion). Compound request: 체크인 좀 부탁드릴게요 layers the formal 부탁드리다 on top, common at luxury properties where deference matters. 체크인해요? as a rising-intonation question to a companion ('shall we check in?') is the polite-suggestion form without any command.

Opening with 체크인할 수 있어요? ('am I able to check in?') sounds like you doubt the hotel can serve you; just declare 체크인할게요. Also, 체크인 is a noun loan-word and must be joined with -하다 to make a verb — writing it as standalone 체크인요 sounds cut short and unnatural.

mistakes: Saying 체크인 있어요? thinking it means 'do you have check-in?' — 있다 asks about existence/availability, which is nonsensical here. Say 체크인할게요 to perform the action.
체크인할게요.
Using 반말 체크인할게 to the front-desk clerk because it's shorter. Staff are strangers, so the -요 is required. Drop the 요 only with a friend.
체크인할게요.
Pronouncing it 'chek-in-hal-ge-yo' but writing 체크인 할게요 with a space — 체크인하다 is one verb, so keep 체크인할게요 together.
체크인할게요.

usage: Polite 존댓말 — telling staff your booking already exists
반말 — to a friend, e.g. 'I booked the hotel already'
격식 — business trip or formal desk, very crisp
Natural extension naming how you booked, invites them to look it up
examples: A: 어서 오세요. / B: 예약했어요. 박지영이에요.
A: Welcome. / B: I have a reservation. It's Park Jiyoung.
Typical arrival exchange — stating the booking and name in two short beats
김민수 이름으로 예약했어요.
I made a reservation under the name Kim Minsu.
Everyday: the two pieces of info staff always need — you booked + whose name
이틀 전에 전화로 예약했는데, 확인 좀 해 주세요.
I booked by phone two days ago — could you check, please?
Real situation: your name isn't showing and you need them to look harder; -는데 explains the context before the request
nuance: 예약했어요 means 'I already made a reservation' — the past tense of 예약하다 signals that the booking exists, so staff know not to treat you as a walk-in. Register is neutral-polite 존댓말; raise it to 예약했습니다 at formal desks, or drop to 예약했어 with friends. The trailing 예약했는데요 ('I booked...') is softer because it leaves a gap the clerk fills, while 예약했어요 is a complete assertion. The important vocabulary contrast: hotels, restaurants, and trains use 예약, while arranging to meet a person (an appointment) uses 약속 — confusing the two is the classic mistake. Do not say the English-loan 'reservation 있어요'; the Korean noun is 예약. And never swap future 예약할게요 ('I'll book now') for this past-tense expression when you mean the booking already exists.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I reserved (it, already)' — the past tense -했어요 is load-bearing: it tells the clerk that the booking exists. Saying the present 예약해요 or the future 예약할게요 instead completely changes what you are communicating.

Neutral-polite (존댓말). Use at any service counter — hotel, restaurant, clinic, airline — where a booking was made ahead of time. 예약했습니다 is the 격식 upgrade for business trips or formal settings. 예약했어 is 반말 for friends only.

예약했는데요 contains the same past-tense assertion but trails off so the clerk takes the next action (looking it up). 예약 있어요 ('I have a booking', noun + 있다) is also natural but slightly less assertive than the verb form. Use 예약했어요 as a confident opener, 예약했는데요 when you want them to search first.

Name: [이름]으로 예약했어요 — 으로 marks whose name the reservation is under, not the destination. Channel: 온라인으로 예약했어요 / 전화로 예약했어요 / 앱으로 예약했어요 — naming how you booked often speeds up the lookup. Party size: 두 명으로 예약했어요 — 으로 again, here meaning 'for two'. At a restaurant, 4인으로 예약했어요 and 2인 2실로 예약했어요 (two rooms for two) are common patterns. All use the same structure: [detail]으로 예약했어요.

The biggest trap is 약속했어요 — 약속 is a promise or social appointment between people, not a service booking. Hotel/restaurant/ticket reservations always use 예약. A second trap: using the present or future form when the booking already exists. It must be past tense: 예약했어요.

mistakes: Saying 약속했어요 to mean 'I have a reservation' — 약속 is a promise/appointment between people, not a room booking. Use 예약했어요 for hotels, restaurants, tickets.
예약했어요.
Using present 예약해요 when you mean it's already done. Korean needs the past -했어요 to show the booking exists. 예약했어요.
예약했어요.
Saying 예약할게요 at the desk thinking it confirms your booking — that means 'I'll book now'. To state an existing booking, use the past 예약했어요.
예약했어요.

english: Do you have a room available?
usage: Do you have a vacant room?
Polite — walk-in guest asking a motel/hotel desk
반말 — asking a friend who works there, or a very casual guesthouse
Do you have a room for tonight?
Natural extension specifying you need it tonight
examples: A: 어서 오세요! / B: 예약은 안 했는데요, 빈방 있어요?
A: Welcome! / B: I didn't book, but do you have a room free?
Prototypical walk-in A/B — admit you have no reservation, then ask; this phrasing is natural and non-abrupt
오늘 하룻밤만 묵으려고 하는데, 빈방 있어요?
I just want to stay one night — do you have a vacancy?
Everyday: late arrival asking for a single-night spot
두 명인데 빈방 있어요? 더블 아니면 트윈 상관없어요.
It's two people — any rooms free? Double or twin is fine.
Real situation: walk-in couple stating headcount and flexibility about bed type
nuance: 빈방 있어요? is literally 'is there an empty room?' — 빈 (empty/vacant) + 방 (room), written as one compound noun. It is the walk-in traveler's first question when no booking was made. Register is standard-polite; 빈방 있습니까? is formal, 빈방 있어? is casual 반말. The key contrast is with 방 있어요? ('do you have a room?'), which omits the vacancy element — add 빈 specifically when you want to signal 'right now, free to give me tonight'. Another everyday phrase, 자리 있어요?, fits restaurants and transport ('is there a seat/spot?') but not lodging rooms; for a place to sleep, 빈방 is the right compound. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'available' with a possibility verb (방 가능해요?) — Korean expresses availability through 있다 (existence), not 가능하다 (possibility). Also keep the rising question intonation: spoken with a falling tone, 빈방 있어요 sounds like a statement.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Is there an empty room?' — 빈 (empty/vacant) modifies 방 (room) as one compound 빈방. The 있다 structure expresses availability through existence ('there is / there isn't'), not through possibility. That is why 방 가능해요? sounds wrong to Korean ears.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use as a walk-in at any hotel, motel, guesthouse, or 펜션. 빈방 있습니까? is the formal upgrade; 빈방 있어? is 반말 for a friend working the desk. Pair with 오늘 밤 (tonight) or 이틀 (two nights) to narrow the request.

방 있어요? drops 빈 and is slightly vaguer — fine once they see you're a walk-in, but 빈방 있어요? is clearer. 자리 있어요? asks about a seat or spot (restaurants, trains) and is wrong for lodging. Do not substitute 빈자리 here.

Time: 오늘 밤 빈방 있어요? / 이번 주말에 빈방 있어요? — 에 attaches to the time expression. Range: 5일부터 7일까지 빈방 있어요? — 부터...까지 spans a date range. Situation: 혼자인데 싱글룸 빈방 있어요? — stating your situation first (혼자인데 / 두 명인데) lets the clerk know which room type to look for. Type upgrade: 비어 있는 방 있어요? is a slightly fuller alternative using the verb phrase 비어 있다 instead of the compound adjective 빈.

Translating 'available' with 가능해요 — 방 가능해요? — is the most common error; Koreans use 있다 for availability. Also, the question only works with rising intonation; 빈방 있어요 said flat sounds like you're stating a fact (there is an empty room), not asking.

mistakes: Asking 방 가능해요? as a literal 'is a room available' — 가능하다 means 'is it possible' and clashes with 방. Use 있다: 빈방 있어요?
빈방 있어요?
Writing 빈 방 with a space and treating 빈 as a separate word every time — the fixed compound 빈방 is most natural here. 빈방 있어요?
빈방 있어요?
Using 자리 있어요? for a hotel room because it worked at a restaurant. 자리 is a seat/spot; a room to sleep in is 방. 빈방 있어요?
빈방 있어요?

usage: Polite — guest to staff or host
반말 + slang 비번 — to a friend or younger host
May I have the Wi-Fi password?
격식 / extra-polite — softer, very common at front desks
Natural extension — first check it exists before asking the password
examples: 와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
What's the Wi-Fi password?
The bare question once you know there's Wi-Fi — subject particle 가 is required for a natural question
A: 와이파이 돼요? / B: 네, 돼요. / A: 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
A: Is there Wi-Fi? / B: Yes, there is. / A: What's the password?
Natural A/B exchange — first confirm it works, then ask the password; this two-step is how Koreans do it in real life
와이파이가 안 잡히는데, 비밀번호가 어떻게 되나요?
I can't pick up the Wi-Fi — could you tell me the password?
Real situation: the network isn't connecting; 어떻게 되나요 is gentler than 뭐예요 when something has already gone wrong
nuance: 와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요? is the everyday polite question a guest asks staff or a host for the Wi-Fi password. The subject particle 가 on 비밀번호 marks it as what is being asked about — dropping it ('비밀번호 뭐예요?') is understood but sounds bare. 비밀번호 (비밀 'secret' + 번호 'number') is the standard polite form; speech shortens it to 비번, acceptable with friends but keep the full form with strangers. The courteous upgrade 어떻게 되나요? ('how does it go?') is what front-desk staff themselves say and sounds less blunt than 뭐예요?. The two questions are interchangeable in meaning but different in feel: 뭐예요 is direct and natural, 어떻게 되나요 is extra-courteous service-register. First ask 와이파이 돼요? to confirm the network works; jumping straight to 비밀번호가 뭐예요? when the signal is absent will get you the code but not solve the problem. Never say '비밀번호를 주세요' — 주다 is for physical objects you hand over, not strings of information.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'As for the Wi-Fi password, what is it?' The subject particle 가 on 비밀번호 is grammatically load-bearing — it marks the thing being asked about. Dropping the particle produces a correct but bare-sounding version; the particle is what makes it natural standard Korean.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use with hotel staff, Airbnb hosts, café staff, or anyone you don't know well. Upgrade to 비밀번호가 어떻게 되나요? at formal or luxury settings — it sounds courteous rather than demanding. 비번 뭐야? is 반말 for friends only; never abbreviate 비밀번호 to 비번 with strangers.

비밀번호가 어떻게 되나요? and 비밀번호가 뭐예요? are essentially synonymous, but the '어떻게 되나요' form sounds gentler and is the version service workers prefer. Use 뭐예요 for directness, 어떻게 되나요 when you want extra courtesy or when following up a problem (Wi-Fi not connecting).

Direct request vs. question: 와이파이 비밀번호 알려 주세요 (tell me please) vs. 비밀번호가 뭐예요? (what is it?) — the request form is softer when someone looks busy. Network scope: 객실 와이파이 비밀번호 (in-room network) vs. 로비 / 공용 와이파이 비밀번호 (lobby/shared network) — at large hotels these are often different codes. Connectivity first: 와이파이가 안 되는데요 ('the Wi-Fi isn't working') + 비밀번호가 맞아요? ('is the password right?') is the natural sequence when the code doesn't work.

Two traps: (1) dropping the particle — 비밀번호 뭐예요? is understandable but unpolished; keep 가. (2) Saying 비밀번호를 주세요 — 주다 is for physical handover; for asking someone to tell you information, use 알려 주세요 or just ask with 뭐예요/어떻게 되나요.

mistakes: Dropping the subject particle: 비밀번호 뭐예요? sounds bare. The natural form marks the subject — 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
Using 비번 with formal staff because you learned it's shorter — 비번 is casual slang. With a clerk, say the full 비밀번호.
와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
Saying 와이파이 돼요? when you actually want the password — that only asks if Wi-Fi exists. To get the code, ask 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요?

usage: Polite — guest checking what the rate covers
반말 — to a travel companion comparing options
격식 — fuller, very polite verb form for a front desk
Do I have to pay separately for breakfast?
Natural extension flipping the question to the cost
examples: 이 가격에 조식 포함이에요?
Is breakfast included in this price?
The most common real form — tie the question to the rate you've just been quoted
A: 조식 포함이에요? / B: 네, 오전 7시부터 10시까지 뷔페로 운영돼요.
A: Is breakfast included? / B: Yes, the buffet runs from 7 to 10 a.m.
Natural A/B: guest asks, clerk confirms and gives the hours — the two questions most travelers want answered
조식 포함이에요? 포함이면 몇 시부터예요?
Is breakfast included? If so, what time does it start?
Real situation: confirming inclusion and checking the opening hour in one breath
nuance: 조식 포함이에요? asks whether breakfast is bundled into the room rate; 포함이에요 is the copula '(it) is included', treating 포함 (包含, inclusion) as a noun and describing the rate with it. 조식 (朝食) is the hotel/formal Sino-Korean word for breakfast — everyday Korean says 아침, but at a hotel counter 조식 is the expected register. The fuller verb form 조식이 포함되어 있나요? uses the passive-progressive 포함되어 있다 ('is included / exists in included state') and sounds more formal and deliberate — staff often say it this way. The nearest alternative, 조식 따로 내야 돼요? ('do I pay extra for breakfast?'), asks the same question from the cost angle; use 포함이에요? to ask whether it's bundled, and 따로 내야 돼요? when you suspect it's extra and want to confirm. A common English-speaker error is 조식 있어요? which asks whether breakfast merely exists, not whether it's free with the room.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'As for breakfast, is it (a) inclusion?' — 포함 is a noun ('inclusion') and 이에요 is the copula. The more formal variant 포함되어 있나요? turns 포함 into a passive verb ('is it in a state of being included?'). Both ask exactly the same thing; the copula version is shorter and more conversational.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use 조식 (Sino-Korean 朝食) at any hotel counter — this is the expected term in hospitality. Everyday speech uses 아침 (아침 식사), but 아침 포함이에요? is less hotel-natural. The 격식 upgrade is 조식이 포함되어 있나요?; 반말 포함이야? is for friends.

조식 따로 내야 돼요? ('do I pay extra for breakfast?') is the complementary question: 포함이에요? asks if it's bundled, 따로 내야 돼요? asks if you'll be charged separately. Use whichever angle fits — both are natural. 조식 있어요? only asks whether breakfast is served at all, not whether it's covered by the rate.

조식(朝食): 朝 (아침 조, morning) + 食 (밥 식, meal). The 朝 character recurs across the meal system: 朝食 breakfast / 中食·점심 lunch / 夕食·석식 dinner — hotel menus use all three. 포함(包含): 包 (쌀 포, to wrap) + 含 (머금을 함, to contain). The opposite 미포함(未包含) or 불포함(不包含) means 'not included'; hearing either on the phone tells you the breakfast is extra. 포함되다 / 포함시키다 are the verb forms: 조식이 포함되어 있다 = it is included (passive-progressive); 조식을 포함시키다 = to add breakfast to the booking.

조식 있어요? sounds like 'is there breakfast?' (does it exist?) rather than 'is it included in the price?' — a very different question. Always use 포함이에요? to ask if it's covered by the rate. A second pitfall: 조식 포함해요? (active 'do you include breakfast?') sounds like asking about the hotel's habit, not the specific rate; stick with the descriptive 포함이에요.

mistakes: Asking 조식 있어요? to mean 'is breakfast included' — that only asks whether breakfast exists. To ask if it's bundled with the rate, say 조식 포함이에요?
조식 포함이에요?
Using 아침 at a hotel desk — it's understood but 조식 is the expected hotel term. 조식 포함이에요?
조식 포함이에요?
Saying 조식 포함해요? (active 'do you include breakfast') — the natural form is the descriptive 포함이에요 or 포함되어 있나요. 조식 포함이에요?
조식 포함이에요?

usage: 반말 — to a friend in the same room
Can I check out a little late?
Natural extension asking for late check-out
examples: 체크아웃 몇 시예요?
What time is check-out?
The bare timing question at any hotel desk — 몇 시 + 예요 with no added particle is the correct natural form
A: 내일 체크아웃 몇 시예요? / B: 정오까지예요.
A: What time is check-out tomorrow? / B: It's until noon.
Classic A/B — guest confirms the deadline the night before, staff gives the cut-off
체크아웃이 몇 시예요? 11시 넘으면 추가 요금 있어요?
What time is check-out? Is there a surcharge if I go past 11?
Real situation: checking the time and the late-check-out penalty in one go
nuance: 체크아웃 몇 시예요? asks for the posted check-out time; 몇 시 ('what time') is directly followed by the copula 예요 with no extra particle — that is how Korean asks 'what time IS it / is X'. The formal version 체크아웃이 몇 시까지인가요? adds 까지 ('until') to stress the hard deadline and -인가요 for extra courtesy. The meaningful contrast between the two: 몇 시예요 asks 'what is the official time', whereas 몇 시까지예요 asks 'what is the latest I can leave' — choose the 까지 form when you suspect you'll be cutting it close. With friends 몇 시야? is fine. The classic particle error is inserting the time-marker 에 and saying 몇 시에예요? — that mixes the action time-marker 에 with the copula 예요 in a way that is grammatically wrong; for 'what time IS X', you simply use 몇 시예요. Also, never use 뭐예요 ('what is it') for a clock time — Korean time questions use 몇 시, not 뭐.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Check-out, what-time is it?' — the copula structure [noun] 몇 시예요 is the standard Korean form for 'what time is [noun]'. No particle sits between 몇 시 and 예요. This contrasts with action sentences (몇 시에 열어요?) where the time-marker 에 IS required.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Ask at check-in or the evening before departure. 체크아웃이 몇 시까지인가요? is the 격식 upgrade that emphasizes the deadline; use it when asking at a business hotel or when you may be running late. 반말 몇 시야? is only between friends sharing a room.

몇 시예요 asks the official posted time. 몇 시까지예요 asks the latest moment you are allowed to leave — more useful if you're planning to sleep in. 늦게 체크아웃 할 수 있어요? is the follow-up question when you want to negotiate a late check-out.

Service register: 체크아웃 시간이 어떻게 돼요? — the polite 어떻게 되다 pattern ('how does it work?') is how staff and guests phrase procedural questions. Late checkout: 체크아웃 좀 늦춰 주실 수 있어요? uses 늦추다 (to delay/push back). 늦게 체크아웃 가능해요? and 레이트 체크아웃 가능해요? are the casual and loan-word variants respectively. Penalty: 늦게 나가면 추가 요금 있어요? — asking if a surcharge applies is the natural follow-up once you know there is a hard cut-off time.

Two distinct errors: (1) Inserting 에 — 몇 시에예요? sounds like you're asking 'at what time?' about an action, but check-out IS a scheduled time, so the copula 예요 alone is correct; no 에 needed. (2) Substituting 뭐예요 — 뭐 asks about the identity of a thing ('what IS it?'), not a clock value; clock questions require 몇 시 ('what number hour'). A third trap: 체크아웃이 언제예요? asks 'when' broadly and could get a date in return — for the specific clock time, stick with 몇 시예요.

mistakes: Saying 체크아웃 몇 시에예요? — you don't add the time-marker 에 before the copula. For 'what time is it', use 몇 시예요. 체크아웃 몇 시예요?
체크아웃 몇 시예요?
Asking 체크아웃 뭐예요? to mean 'what time' — 뭐 is 'what (thing)', not a clock time. Clock times use 몇 시. 체크아웃 몇 시예요?
체크아웃 몇 시예요?
Reading 몇 시 as written 'myeot si' but it sounds 'myeot ssi' — pronunciation aside, keep the spelling 몇 시 with a space. 체크아웃 몇 시예요?
체크아웃 몇 시예요?

english: Can I leave my bags here?
usage: Polite — guest to desk, 좀 softens the ask
반말 — to a friend at the counter, rare with staff
Could I possibly leave my bags?
격식 / extra-polite — -ㄹ까요 makes the request gentler
체크인 전까지 짐 좀 맡아 주세요.
Please hold my bags until check-in.
Natural extension as a direct request to keep them
examples: 방이 아직 준비 안 됐으면 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
If the room isn't ready yet, can I leave my bags?
Early-arrival ask — the conditional makes it sound considerate rather than demanding
A: 체크아웃했는데 비행기가 저녁이라서요. / B: 짐 맡아 드릴게요.
A: I've checked out but my flight isn't until the evening. / B: We'll hold your bags for you.
The classic late-flight exchange — guest implies the need, staff offers proactively with 맡아 드릴게요 (the staff's own 주다 form)
짐이 좀 많은데, 몇 시간 맡길 수 있어요?
I have quite a few bags — can I leave them for a few hours?
Real situation: specifying duration so staff know how long to store them
nuance: 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요? asks hotel staff to store your luggage temporarily; 맡기다 is 'to entrust (something to someone for safekeeping)', and 좀 makes the request polite rather than demanding. Register is standard-polite; soften to 맡길 수 있을까요? for extra courtesy. The crucial verb pair: 맡기다 (you hand your bags over to them) vs 맡다 (they accept responsibility for them) — from the guest's side you always 맡기다. The direct-request alternative 짐 좀 맡아 주세요 ('please look after my bags') skips the ability question and asks outright; use the 맡길 수 있어요? form when you're not sure they offer this service, 맡아 주세요 when you know they do. English speakers often reach for 두다/놓다 ('to place/put down'), producing 짐 둘 수 있어요? — that only asks if you can set bags on the floor, not if someone will guard them. The 좀 must stay; removing it shifts the sentence from a polite request to a blunt demand.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Can I entrust my bags?' — 맡기다 is the verb for handing something to someone for safekeeping, not merely placing it somewhere. This is why 짐 둘 수 있어요? ('can I put my bags down?') is the wrong verb: it describes physical placement, not entrusting.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use at hotel check-in (room not ready yet) or after check-out (late flight). 맡길 수 있을까요? is the extra-polite version for higher-end hotels. Never use 반말 with staff; 맡길 수 있어? is only for a companion who works there.

짐 맡아 주세요 is the direct-request alternative ('please hold my bags') — use it when you already know they offer luggage storage. 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요? is the permission-seeking version — use it when you are unsure. The meaning is the same; the framing differs.

Time frame: 체크인 전까지 맡길 수 있어요? (before check-in) / 체크아웃 후에 몇 시간만 맡길 수 있어요? (a few hours after check-out) — 까지 and 후에 anchor the storage window. Quantity: 가방 두 개 맡길 수 있어요? — counting bags with 개. Service enquiry: 짐 보관 서비스 있어요? or 코인 로커 있어요? (coin locker) are both real options to check first; coin lockers are common at Korean stations. Pickup: 짐 맡겨 놨는데, 찾으러 왔어요 — 맡겨 놓다 (to leave in storage) and 찾으러 오다 (to come to retrieve) are the natural pair for the collection.

짐 둘 수 있어요? uses 두다 (to place/put), which asks permission to set bags on the floor — not to have them guarded. The safekeeping verb is 맡기다. Also, omitting 좀 (짐 맡길 수 있어요?) is grammatically correct but sounds blunt; 좀 is the social lubricant that makes this a genuine request.

mistakes: Saying 짐 둘 수 있어요? ('can I put my bags down') for storage — 두다 is just placing. To have them safely held, use 맡기다: 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
Mixing up 맡다 and 맡기다: 맡기다 = you hand it over, 맡다 = they take it on. As the guest entrusting bags, you 맡기다. 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
Dropping 좀 and saying 짐 맡길 수 있어요? — it's grammatical but blunt. 좀 turns it into a courteous request. 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?

usage: 반말 — a friend joking, or peer to peer; not used by officials
Could you show me your passport?
Please show your passport and boarding pass.
Natural extension asking for both documents
examples: 여권 보여 주세요.
Please show me your passport.
The bare line an official says at a check-in counter or immigration booth
A: 체크인하시려면 여권 보여 주세요. / B: 여기 있어요.
A: To check in, please show me your passport. / B: Here you go.
Typical A/B at an airline desk — the phrase you will hear most often as a traveler and should be ready to respond to
여권 보여 주세요. 그리고 손가락 여기에 올려 주세요.
Please show your passport. And place your finger here.
Real immigration encounter: two polite -아/어 주세요 requests in sequence — important to understand as a traveler
nuance: 여권 보여 주세요 is what an airline clerk, hotel, or immigration officer says to request sight of a passport; as a traveler you mostly hear this, but you apply the same -아/어 주세요 pattern to make any polite request of your own. 보여 주다 is 'to show (someone something)', literally 'do the favor of causing (it) to be seen'. The critical verb distinction: 보여 주세요 asks only to display the passport, while 여권 주세요 asks the person to physically hand it over for the official to hold — if you only need to see it, use 보여 주세요. Another easily confused form is 봐 주세요: 봐 주다 means 'do me the favor of watching/looking after', so 여권 봐 주세요 would mean 'please look after my passport', not 'show it to me'. Upgrade to 보여 주시겠어요? for softer courtesy; use 보여 줘 only with friends.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Please do the favor of making (it) seen' — 보이다 is the causative of 보다 ('to see'), so 보여 주다 = 'cause it to be visible for me'. This is why the spacing is 보여 주세요 (two words): 보여 is the causative stem, 주세요 is the favor verb.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Heard most at airports, hotels, and immigration desks — both spoken to you and by you when you need documents from someone. 보여 주시겠어요? is the extra-courteous upgrade typical of formal officials. 보여 줘 is 반말 reserved for friends.

여권 주세요 asks the person to physically hand the passport to the official (who then holds it). 여권 보여 주세요 only asks for a visual display — the traveler keeps the document. Choose 주세요 for hand-over, 보여 주세요 for show-only.

Documents combined: 여권이랑 탑승권 보여 주세요 — 이랑 links nouns casually (보다 formal: 여권과 탑승권). ID swap: 신분증 보여 주세요 — 신분증 (ID card) replaces 여권 at domestic counters; pattern is identical. Polite softening: 보여 주시겠어요? raises the courtesy a full level. Reciprocal situation: as a traveler, 비자 보여 주세요 and 예방접종 증명서 보여 주세요 apply the same 보이다 + 주다 pattern to other travel documents.

봐 주세요 and 보여 주세요 look similar but are completely different: 봐 주세요 = 'please take care of (watch over)'; 보여 주세요 = 'please show'. Using 봐 주세요 for passport display is a serious error. Remember: 보여 = causative, 봐 = plain past/stem.

mistakes: Saying 여권 봐 주세요 to mean 'show your passport' — 봐 주다 means 'look after / do me the favor of watching'. To display it, use 보여 주세요.
여권 보여 주세요.
Confusing 여권 주세요 (hand it over) with 여권 보여 주세요 (just show it). If you only need to see it, add 보여. 여권 보여 주세요.
여권 보여 주세요.
Writing 보여주세요 as one chunk or forcing 여권을 — natural spoken form drops 을 and spaces 보여 주세요. 여권 보여 주세요.
여권 보여 주세요.

usage: 반말 — to the friend you're flying with
격식 — native term 탑승구 + formal ending
Natural extension giving the gate number and asking direction
examples: 죄송한데, 34번 게이트가 어디예요?
Excuse me — where is gate 34?
The most natural real opener: apologize briefly to stop someone, then give the gate number
A: 탑승 시간이 다 됐는데, 게이트가 어디예요? / B: 저쪽 끝으로 쭉 가시면 돼요.
A: It's almost boarding time — where's the gate? / B: Just keep going all the way to the far end.
Rushing A/B exchange — the urgency shows in the -는데 clause, the reply gives a direction
인천공항인데 탑승구가 어디인가요? 게이트 번호가 달라서요.
I'm at Incheon Airport — where is the boarding gate? The gate number seems different.
Real situation: a discrepancy on the boarding pass causes confusion; uses the formal 탑승구 because it matches signage
nuance: 게이트가 어디예요? asks airport staff or a fellow traveler where the boarding gate is; the loanword 게이트 is universally understood in airports while the official signage term is 탑승구 (탑승 'boarding' + 구 'mouth/opening'). Both mean the same physical gate, but 게이트 is what you say, 탑승구 is what you read on boards. Register is standard-polite; the subject particle 가 marks 게이트 before the location copula 어디예요. 탑승구가 어디인가요? is the formal upgrade. The key contrast with the direction alternative 게이트 어느 쪽이에요? ('which way is the gate?'): use 어디예요 when you genuinely don't know where the gate is, 어느 쪽이에요 when you know the general area and just need left/right. A common English-speaker error is jumping to 게이트 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to the gate?'), which presumes you know the destination — use 어디예요 to locate it first, then 어떻게 가요 if the route is complicated.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'As for the gate, where is it?' — 어디예요 is the location copula ('where IS it'), not 어디 있어요 ('where does it exist'). Both work for a fixed place; 어디예요 is the more concise spoken form at an airport.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use with airport staff, fellow travelers, or info desks. 탑승구가 어디인가요? is the 격식 version that matches signage language — useful when your boarding pass shows 탑승구 and you need to ask. 반말 어디야? is only for friends.

어디예요 = where is it (location unknown). 어느 쪽이에요 = which direction (rough area known). 어떻게 가요 = how do I get there (you know the destination but not the route). Sequence matters: find it (어디예요), then navigate (어느 쪽/어떻게).

Gate number: n번 게이트가 어디예요? — 번 attaches to the number (34번 게이트). Terminal: 제2터미널 게이트 어디예요? — critical at Incheon, which has two separate terminals; 제1/제2터미널 must be confirmed on the boarding pass. Signs: 탑승구 표지판이 어디예요? — when the gate zone is unknown, finding the sign first is the practical first step. Direction narrowing: 게이트 어느 쪽이에요? — use once you know the general concourse but need left vs. right; this is the natural follow-up to 어디예요?

게이트 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to the gate?') is an error when you don't yet know WHERE the gate is — it presumes you know the destination. Establish location first with 어디예요, then ask the route if needed. A second trap: reading the sign 탑승구 but not recognizing spoken 게이트 — know both terms.

mistakes: Asking 게이트 어떻게 가요? before you know where it is — that asks the route, not the location. Find it first: 게이트가 어디예요?
게이트가 어디예요?
Dropping the particle: 게이트 어디예요? is OK casually, but the polished form marks the subject. 게이트가 어디예요?
게이트가 어디예요?
Reading signage 탑승구 and then not recognizing spoken 게이트 — they mean the same gate. Either works: 게이트가 어디예요?
게이트가 어디예요?

usage: Polite — customer at a bank or exchange booth
반말 — to a friend, not to the teller
I'd like to exchange some money...
격식-ish / softer — trails off so the teller takes over
I'd like to change dollars into won.
examples: 환전하고 싶어요. 달러에서 원으로요.
I'd like to exchange money — dollars to won.
The cleanest opener at an exchange counter: state the desire, then immediately specify the direction of conversion
A: 어떻게 도와드릴까요? / B: 환전하려고 하는데요, 오늘 환율이 어떻게 돼요?
A: How can I help you? / B: I'd like to exchange money — what's today's rate?
Natural A/B at a bank: -려고 하는데요 trails off so the teller starts talking; then ask the rate before committing
100달러 환전하고 싶어요. 소액권으로 주실 수 있어요?
I'd like to exchange 100 dollars. Can you give me small bills?
Real situation: state the amount, then specify the denomination — both are normal follow-ups
nuance: 환전하고 싶어요 tells a teller or exchange booth that you want to exchange currency; 환전(換錢, 換 'swap' + 錢 'money') is the specific banking term for currency exchange plus -하다, and -고 싶어요 declares your own desire. Register is standard-polite; many people prefer 환전하려고 하는데요, which softens the bluntness of stating a bare desire and invites the teller to guide the transaction. The everyday alternative 돈 좀 바꾸고 싶어요 uses the plain verb 바꾸다 ('to swap/change') — it's fully understood but less precise at a financial counter, where 환전 is the correct term. The crucial vocabulary warning: 교환(交換) means exchanging goods or returns (like at a store), not currencies — never say 교환하고 싶어요 for money. And -고 싶어요 can only express the speaker's own desire; you cannot use it to ask 'do you want' about someone else.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I want to do money-exchange' — 환전 is the set noun for currency exchange and attaches -하다 as a verb. The -고 싶어요 ending belongs exclusively to the speaker's own desires; it cannot express another person's wants the way English 'want' can.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use at airport exchange booths, bank teller windows, or hotel front desks that offer currency exchange. 환전하려고 하는데요 is the softer, service-appropriate variant — it trails off and lets the teller take over. 반말 환전하고 싶어 is only for friends.

돈 좀 바꾸고 싶어요 uses 바꾸다 (plain 'to swap') — natural in any context, but 환전 is the precise financial term you'd use at a counter. 환전하려고 하는데요 is the softer opener when you want the teller to lead. Both mean the same thing; they differ in register and who drives the conversation.

환전(換錢): 換 (바꿀 환, to swap/exchange) + 錢 (돈 전, money). 換 is the source of the confusion: 교환(交換) = 交(사귈 교, interact) + 換 = exchange of goods between parties; 환전(換錢) = swap + money = currency exchange. Both share 換 but differ in what is swapped. 錢 (돈 전) is an archaic character for money, survives mainly in compounds: 환전, 용돈(用錢, pocket money), 세뱃돈은 錢이 아닌 순우리말. Knowing these roots helps you predict that 환율(換率, exchange rate) shares the same 換.

교환하고 싶어요 is the most common error — 교환 is 'exchange of goods/returns' (e.g. returning a shirt), not currency. Also, -고 싶어요 only works for first-person desire; using it for 'do you want to exchange?' is grammatically wrong (use -고 싶으세요? if you need to ask).

mistakes: Saying 교환하고 싶어요 for currency — 교환 means swapping goods/returns. Money exchange is 환전: 환전하고 싶어요.
환전하고 싶어요.
Using -고 싶어요 to ask the teller 'do you want' — -고 싶다 states only your own desire. For your request, keep it first-person: 환전하고 싶어요.
환전하고 싶어요.
Saying 환전 있어요? expecting to exchange — 있다 asks if exchange 'exists'. State your intent: 환전하고 싶어요.
환전하고 싶어요.

english: Could you take a photo for me?
usage: Could you take a photo for me?
Polite/courteous — asking a stranger a favor
Sorry, but could you take a photo?
격식 — adding 죄송한데 to a stranger makes it gentler
Natural extension explaining how, after they agree
examples: 죄송한데, 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
Sorry to bother you, but could you take a photo for us?
The most natural real-world opener — preface with 죄송한데 when stopping a stranger; this small apology makes the request far more natural
A: 저희 둘이 같이 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요? / B: 네, 물론이죠!
A: Could you take a photo of the two of us together? / B: Of course!
The complete exchange — couple asks a passerby, who agrees; 저희 둘이 makes it clear both people should be in frame
저기 배경 나오게 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요? 저기까지 다 나오면 좋겠어요.
Could you take a photo with that background in it? It'd be great if you could get all the way over there in the shot.
Real situation: giving framing instructions to your volunteer photographer
nuance: 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요? is how you ask a stranger to photograph you; -아/어 주시겠어요 is the highest-courtesy request form ('would you do the favor of...') and is exactly right for imposing on someone you don't know. 좀 softens it further. Dropping to 찍어 주세요 is still polite but slightly more direct; 찍어 줘 is 반말 for friends only. The critical verb distinction: 찍다 = active 'to take a photo' (what the person you ask does), whereas 찍히다 = passive 'to get photographed' (what happens to you) — so the favor form must use the active 찍어 주다. The near-synonym 사진 좀 찍어 주실 수 있어요? ('would you be able to...') is essentially the same courtesy level. The English-speaker trap is 사진 찍을 수 있어요? — that asks about physical ability ('are you capable of taking a photo?'), not for a favor; 주시겠어요/주세요 is what makes it a polite request. Forgetting 주다 produces 사진 찍으세요, which commands THEM to photograph something for themselves — the opposite of your intention.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Would you do the favor of pressing the shutter?' — 주시겠어요 is the highest-courtesy 주다 ending, conveying 'would you do this for me?'. The 찍어 is the stem of 찍다 ('to take/shoot'), not the passive 찍히다 ('to get photographed'). The direction of the favor (you asking them to shoot you) requires the active form.

Courteous-polite — exactly calibrated for asking a stranger at a tourist spot. Add 죄송한데 at the start to soften the interruption further. Drop to 찍어 주세요 with someone you've been chatting with. Use 반말 찍어 줘 only with friends.

사진 좀 찍어 주실 수 있어요? ('would you be able to take a photo?') is essentially the same politeness level. 사진 찍어 주세요 is slightly more direct — still polite, but doesn't have the deferential 겠 ('would'). Neither is wrong; 주시겠어요 is the safest choice with a stranger.

Instructions after agreement: 여기 버튼만 누르시면 돼요 (just press this button) — the -시면 돼요 pattern ('you just need to -') is the polite way to explain a simple action to a helper. Framing: 저 배경이랑 같이 나오게 찍어 주세요 — 나오다 ('to come out/appear') is the standard verb for what appears in a photo. Repeat: 한 장 더 찍어 주시겠어요? — 한 장 더 adds 'one more shot'. Orientation: 세로로 / 가로로 찍어 주세요 — portrait vs. landscape, useful for tall landmarks.

사진 찍을 수 있어요? questions their physical capability — 'are you capable of taking a photo?' Strangers find this odd. To ask a favor, use 주시겠어요/주세요. Forgetting 주다 entirely (사진 찍으세요) is an even bigger error — it orders them to take a photo for themselves.

mistakes: Saying 사진 찍을 수 있어요? to ask the favor — that questions their ability. Use the favor pattern: 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
Dropping 주다 and saying 사진 찍으세요 — that orders them to take a photo (for themselves). To have them shoot YOU, keep 찍어 주다: 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
Mixing 찍히다 (get photographed) with 찍다 (take a photo). The helper 찍다 the photo. 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?

usage: Polite — asking staff or a passerby
격식 — fuller 'should I' phrasing, very polite
Where do I buy the admission ticket?
Natural extension swapping in 입장권 for an attraction
examples: 지하철 표는 어디서 사요?
Where do I buy subway tickets?
The most common real use — add 지하철/KTX/영화관 before 표 to specify what kind of ticket
A: 표는 어디서 사요? / B: 저기 자동발매기에서 사시면 돼요.
A: Where do I buy tickets? / B: You can buy them at that vending machine over there.
Typical A/B at a station — asking a stranger who points to the machine; 자동발매기 (automatic ticket machine) is the word you need to understand in reply
줄이 두 개인데, 표는 어디서 사요?
There are two lines — which one is for buying tickets?
Real situation: confused by separate queues; 표 + 어디서 사요 elegantly collapses the question
nuance: 표는 어디서 사요? asks where to purchase tickets; 에서 (contracted to 서 in speech) marks the PLACE where an action is performed, so 어디서 사요 = 'at which place do (I) buy'. The topic particle 는 on 표 sets 'tickets' as the subject we're discussing, which also implies a mild contrast ('as for tickets, specifically'). Register is standard-polite; 어디서 사야 하나요? adds the obligation nuance 'where SHOULD I buy' for extra courtesy. 표 covers tickets broadly; at an attraction or museum the specific word is 입장권 (admission ticket), at a train station it's 승차권 or just 표. The alternative phrasing 표 어디서 파는지 아세요? ('do you know where they sell tickets?') is gentler for stopping a random stranger — it asks about their knowledge rather than demanding information. The key grammar trap is 에 vs 에서: buying is an action and needs the action-location marker 에서, not the static-location 에 (어디에 사요? is wrong).

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'As for tickets, where does one buy them?' — 어디서 is 어디 + 에서 contracted; 에서 marks the place of an action ('at which place'). This is not the same as 에 (static location). The topic marker 는 on 표 frames 'tickets' as the subject under discussion, subtly implying you may already know other things but want to clarify this specifically.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use at stations, airports, cinemas, tourist attractions. 표는 어디서 사야 하나요? is the polite-formal upgrade with 'should I' nuance. 반말 표 어디서 사? is for friends. Note 표 is the general word; say 입장권 for an attraction's entry ticket, 승차권 for transport.

표 어디서 파는지 아세요? ('do you know where tickets are sold?') is softer for a random stranger — it frames the question as asking about their knowledge, not commanding information. 표는 어디서 사요 is more direct and appropriate with staff. Both are correct; choose based on who you're asking.

Transport: KTX 표는 어디서 사요? uses the same 어디서+사다 skeleton. Machine: 자동발매기 어디에 있어요? — note 있어요 takes 에 (static location), not 에서, because you're asking where the machine exists, not where to perform an action. Attraction: 입장권은 어디서 사요? — 입장권 for entry tickets. Online: 온라인으로도 살 수 있어요? — 으로 marks the means; 도 adds 'also'. 어디서 파는지 아세요? — softer stranger form ('do you know where they sell them?') avoids sounding demanding.

어디에 사요? uses the static-location particle 에 — buying is an action, so 에서 (action location) is required. 어디 사요? with no particle sounds incomplete. These are two different but common errors; always use 어디서 with action verbs like 사다, 먹다, 만나다.

mistakes: Saying 표는 어디에 사요? — buying is an action, so it needs 에서/서, not the static location 에. 표는 어디서 사요?
표는 어디서 사요?
Dropping the particle: 표 어디 사요? sounds incomplete. Use 어디서 for the place of an action. 표는 어디서 사요?
표는 어디서 사요?
Saying 표 어디 있어요? to mean 'where do I buy' — that asks where tickets are located, not where to purchase. To buy, use 어디서 사요. 표는 어디서 사요?
표는 어디서 사요?

usage: Polite — visitor at a ticket window
How much is the entrance fee?
How much is admission per adult?
Natural extension asking the adult price
examples: 어른 두 명인데 입장료가 얼마예요?
It's two adults — how much is admission?
Everyday: stating headcount first is natural and helps the ticket seller quote the right total
A: 아이는 무료예요? 어른 입장료가 얼마예요? / B: 아이는 무료고요, 어른은 한 명에 12,000원이에요.
A: Are kids free? How much is adult admission? / B: Kids are free, and adults are 12,000 won each.
Family arrival A/B — two questions in one turn, staff answers both; listen for 무료 (free) and the number
청소년 할인이 있어요? 어른 입장료랑 얼마 차이 나요?
Is there a student discount? How much difference is there from the adult admission?
Real situation: asking about a discount tier and comparing it to the regular adult price
nuance: 입장료가 얼마예요? asks the admission fee at a museum, palace, theme park, or any ticketed attraction; 입장료(入場料, 입장 'entry' + 료 'fee/charge') is the precise term for an entry fee and the subject particle 가 marks it before 얼마예요 ('how much is it'). The formal upgrade 입장료가 얼마인가요? sounds more deliberate; 입장료 얼마야? is 반말. The important vocabulary boundary: 입장료 is the fee/charge itself (the price), while 입장권 is the physical or digital ticket — ask 입장료가 얼마예요? for the cost, 입장권은 어디서 사요? for where to buy the ticket. Distinguish also 입장료 (entry fee) from 요금 (general service charge/fare, e.g. 버스 요금) and 가격/값 (price of goods bought, e.g. 커피 가격). The English-speaker error is dropping 료 and asking 입장 얼마예요?, which is incomplete, or asking 비싸요? ('is it expensive?') when what you need is the actual number.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'As for the entry fee, how much is it?' — 입장료 is the fee itself (the number), not the ticket (입장권, the document). 료 (料) means 'charge/fee', so dropping it to 입장 얼마예요? leaves the noun incomplete. 가 is the subject particle: 입장료가 얼마예요 = 'what amount is the entry fee?'

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use at ticket booths, reception desks of attractions, or when calling ahead. 입장료가 얼마인가요? is the 격식 upgrade for formal or upscale venues. 반말 얼마야? is only for friends. Add 어른 / 아이 / 청소년 before 입장료 to ask about specific pricing tiers.

입장권이 얼마예요? is nearly identical but focuses on the ticket (the document/card), not the fee. In practice both are used for 'how much does it cost to get in', but if staff are asking you to pay first and get the ticket later, 입장료 is more precise. Also do not confuse with 요금 (fare/service charge for ongoing services like buses) or 가격 (price of a purchasable item).

입장료(入場料): 入 (들 입, to enter) + 場 (마당 장, venue/place) + 料 (헤아릴 료, measure/fee). The 料 character also appears in 요금 (料金), which is why both relate to charges — but 요금 is a recurring or service fee, 입장료 is a one-time entry charge.

Dropping 료 and saying 입장 얼마예요? sounds incomplete — the head noun needs 료. Asking 비싸요? ('is it expensive?') when you need the actual figure asks for a subjective judgment, not a number; 얼마예요? is what gets you the price.

mistakes: Saying 입장 얼마예요? without 료 — that's incomplete. The fee word is 입장료. 입장료가 얼마예요?
입장료가 얼마예요?
Confusing 입장권 (the ticket) with 입장료 (the fee). To ask the cost, use 입장료. 입장료가 얼마예요?
입장료가 얼마예요?
Asking 입장료 비싸요? when you want the number — that asks if it's expensive. For the amount, use 얼마예요. 입장료가 얼마예요?
입장료가 얼마예요?

english: Is there a good restaurant nearby?
usage: Is there a good restaurant nearby?
Polite — asking a local, host, or hotel staff
이 근처에 맛집 좀 추천해 주시겠어요?
Could you recommend a good restaurant nearby?
격식 / courteous — asking for a recommendation
Is there a place locals go to nearby?
Natural extension asking for a local favorite
examples: 이 동네 처음인데, 근처에 맛집 있어요?
It's my first time in this neighborhood — any good places nearby?
Admitting you're new lowers the social barrier and often gets warmer, more detailed advice
A: 근처에 맛집 있어요? 한식이면 좋겠어요. / B: 이 길 따라 5분 걷다 보면 삼겹살집이 하나 있는데 거기 진짜 맛있어요.
A: Is there a good restaurant nearby? Korean food would be great. / B: If you walk five minutes down this street there's a samgyeopsal place — it's really good.
Natural A/B: stating a cuisine preference gets you a specific recommendation; the reply uses -다 보면 ('if you walk along') which is common in giving directions
저녁 먹으려고 하는데, 현지인들이 자주 가는 맛집 있어요? 관광객 식당 말고요.
I'm looking for dinner — is there a place locals actually go? Not a touristy one.
Real situation: the tourist explicitly asks for a local spot, not a tourist-trap restaurant; 관광객 식당 말고요 ('not a tourist restaurant') is a natural qualifier
nuance: 근처에 맛집 있어요? asks a local, your hotel concierge, or a host whether there is a restaurant worth eating at nearby; 맛집 is the cherished everyday compound for 'a place famous for tasty food' (맛 'taste' + 집 'house/shop'), and 에 on 근처 marks where you want it to exist. Register is standard-polite. If you want a personal recommendation rather than a yes/no, pivot to 맛집 좀 추천해 주시겠어요? ('could you recommend...') — that makes the person name a specific place. English speakers instinctively say 좋은 식당 있어요? ('is there a good restaurant?') which is grammatically fine but feels flat — 맛집 implies specifically 'a place worth going to for the food', a cultural concept Koreans take seriously. Do not ask 맛집 어디 있어요? before confirming one exists; 있어요? ('is there one?') is the correct opener, then 어디예요? gets the location. Also, 맛집 맛있어요? ('is the tasty-place tasty?') is redundant since the 맛 is already in the word.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Near here, is there a tasty-place?' — 맛집 is not just 'a restaurant' but a place with a reputation for good food; locals use it for places they genuinely recommend. Saying 식당 있어요? ('is there a restaurant?') only asks if a dining establishment exists — 맛집 adds the qualitative 'worth eating at' meaning.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Best asked of hotel staff, Airbnb hosts, or a friendly-looking local. 맛집 좀 추천해 주시겠어요? is the more courteous request form that invites a specific recommendation instead of a yes/no. 반말 맛집 있어? is only for friends.

근처에 맛집 있어요? = 'Is there a good eatery nearby?' (existence question, yes/no). 이 근처 맛집 좀 추천해 주시겠어요? = 'Please name a good place nearby' (recommendation request, expects a specific answer). Use 있어요? to open, 추천해 주세요 when you want them to commit to a choice.

Cuisine: 근처에 한식/일식/횟집 맛집 있어요? — drop the cuisine type right before 맛집. Distance: 걸어갈 수 있는 거리에 맛집 있어요? — 걸어갈 수 있는 거리 ('walkable distance') is a set phrase; 걸어서 5분 거리에 맛집 있어요? is the tighter form. Type: 현지인들이 가는 맛집 ('a place locals go') vs. 줄 서는 맛집 ('a place people queue for') — the second implies it's worth waiting. Recommendation pivot: 맛집 좀 추천해 주시겠어요? shifts from asking whether one exists to asking them to name it.

좋은 식당 있어요? is grammatically correct but culturally flat — 맛집 is the word Koreans use when they want to eat somewhere good. Using 좋은 식당 makes you sound like you're asking from a phrasebook rather than talking like a local. Also, 맛집 맛있어요? is redundant (the 맛 is already in the word).

mistakes: Saying 좋은 식당 있어요? — grammatical but flat. The natural word for a tasty, recommended spot is 맛집. 근처에 맛집 있어요?
근처에 맛집 있어요?
Dropping 에: 근처 맛집 있어요? is understandable but 근처에 with the location particle is cleaner. 근처에 맛집 있어요?
근처에 맛집 있어요?
Asking 맛집 맛있어요? thinking it intensifies — 맛집 already means 'tasty place', so that's redundant. Just ask if one exists: 근처에 맛집 있어요?
근처에 맛집 있어요?

usage: 격식 — fuller, slightly more formal ending
examples: 내일 아침에 몇 시에 문 열어요?
What time do you open tomorrow morning?
The most common real form — add 내일 아침에 to confirm for the next day's plan
A: 몇 시에 문 열어요? / B: 오전 10시에 열어요.
A: What time do you open? / B: We open at 10 a.m.
Clean A/B exchange — note 에 in the reply too (열어요 = action, so 10시에 = 'at 10')
주말에도 몇 시에 문 열어요? 평일이랑 시간이 같아요?
What time do you open on weekends too? Is it the same as weekdays?
Real situation: checking whether weekend hours differ — very practical before making a trip
nuance: 몇 시에 문 열어요? asks a shop, museum, or restaurant what time it opens; 에 here is the time-point marker ('at what time') attached to the action verb 열다 ('to open'). 문 열다 ('open the door') is the idiomatic phrase for a business opening for the day — you can drop 문 and just say 몇 시에 열어요?, but keeping 문 sounds natural and specific. The formal variant 문 여나요? replaces the plain -어요 ending with -나요, adding slight distance and courtesy. The all-important grammar contrast with check-out time: 체크아웃 몇 시예요 uses the COPULA (no 에 needed), while 몇 시에 문 열어요 uses an ACTION VERB (에 is required) — this is one of the most confusing pairs for learners. Passive 문이 열려요 describes a door physically swinging open; for regular business hours always use active 문 열어요. The closing counterpart is 몇 시에 문 닫아요? and the rest-day question is 무슨 요일에 쉬어요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'At what time do (you) open the door?' — 문 열다 is the idiom for a business opening. The 에 after 몇 시 is the time-point marker required with action verbs ('AT' a time). Compare: 체크아웃 몇 시예요 (copula, no 에) vs 몇 시에 열어요 (action verb, 에 required) — this is the core contrast.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use with any shop, cafe, museum, attraction, or government office. 문 여나요? is a touch more formal, appropriate for official venues. 반말 문 열어? is for friends. The natural pair: 몇 시에 문 열어요? / 몇 시에 문 닫아요? (opening and closing hours).

영업 몇 시에 시작해요? ('when does the business start?') is a formal alternative using the noun 영업 (business operation). 언제 열어요? asks 'when' more loosely and could get a day-of-week answer rather than a clock time. Use 몇 시에 when you want a specific clock-time answer.

Closing pair: 몇 시에 문 닫아요? mirrors the opening question exactly — 닫다 (to close) takes the same 에 + action-verb structure. Duration: 오늘 몇 시까지 해요? — 까지 ('until') asks for the deadline rather than the opening time; use this when you're already inside. Weekends: 주말에도 열어요? — 에도 = 'even on'; 주말 hours often differ. Days off: 무슨 요일에 쉬어요? — 쉬다 (to rest/be closed) is the natural word for a business's day off, not 닫다. All four form a family of hours-related questions with identical grammar.

The classic error: dropping 에 and saying 몇 시 문 열어요? Learners drop 에 because 체크아웃 몇 시예요 (copula) takes no particle. But 열다 is an action verb and MUST have 에. Active 열어요 vs passive 열려요 is a second trap: 문이 열려요 means a door physically opens (like a sliding door); for business hours, always say 문 열어요 (active).

mistakes: Saying 몇 시 문 열어요? without 에 — action verbs need the time-marker 에 ('at what time'). 몇 시에 문 열어요?
몇 시에 문 열어요?
Confusing this with the copula case (체크아웃 몇 시예요, no 에). With the verb 열다 you DO add 에. 몇 시에 문 열어요?
몇 시에 문 열어요?
Using passive 문이 열려요 for business hours — that describes a door physically opening. For opening time, use active 문 열어요. 몇 시에 문 열어요?
몇 시에 문 열어요?

hangul: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요
english: Please tell me how to get to the airport.
usage: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
Please tell me the way to the airport.
Polite — asking staff or a passerby
공항 가는 길 좀 알려 줘.
Tell me how to get to the airport.
공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
Could you tell me how to get to the airport?
격식 / courteous — softer favor-ask to a stranger
How do I get to the airport?
Natural extension — the common 'how do I get to' phrasing
examples: 죄송한데, 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the airport?
The most natural stranger-stop opener — 죄송한데 softens the interruption, -시겠어요 shows respect
A: 비행기 시간이 얼마 안 남았는데, 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요. / B: 저기 버스 정류장에서 6001번 타시면 돼요.
A: My flight's soon — please tell me how to get to the airport. / B: Take bus 6001 from that stop over there.
Urgent A/B: -는데 clause signals the problem, the reply gives a concrete transport option
여기서 인천공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요. 버스로 가면 얼마나 걸려요?
Please tell me how to get to Incheon Airport from here. How long does it take by bus?
Real situation: specify the airport name and immediately ask for the travel time — both are practical follow-ups
nuance: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 asks someone to explain the route to the airport; 가는 길 is the nominalised phrase for 'the way (one) goes to / the route to', and 알려 주다 ('do the favor of informing me') with 좀 makes it a polite request. Register is standard-polite; the softest form for a stranger is 알려 주시겠어요?, a full -시겠어요 courtesy upgrade. The verb to use is 알려 주다 ('to inform'), NOT 가르쳐 주다 — 가르치다 means 'to teach a subject' (like a school class) and sounds odd for giving directions. The quick-and-casual alternative, 공항 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to the airport?'), asks for the method in one short phrase — use 가는 길 알려 주세요 when you want them to walk you step-by-step through the route, 어떻게 가요 when a brief method ('take the subway') is enough. Do not drop 좀; it's the social lubricant that distinguishes a polite favor from a command.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Please inform me of the going-route for the airport' — 가는 길 is a nominalized phrase: 가는 (present-tense modifier of 가다) + 길 (road/route) = 'the route one takes (to get somewhere)'. 알려 주다 means 'inform / let know', not 가르치다 ('teach'). These two verbs are the key distinction in this expression.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use with hotel concierge, taxi drivers, locals, or info desks. Soften to 알려 주시겠어요? for a stranger you stop on the street. 반말 알려 줘 is for friends only. Do not omit 좀 — it turns the request from a polite favor into a blunt command.

공항 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to the airport?') is shorter and asks for the method — appropriate when you have time and the answer might be 'take subway line 5'. 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 implies you want a step-by-step explanation. Use the former for a quick answer, the latter when genuinely lost and wanting guidance.

Airport specified: 인천공항 / 김포공항 가는 길 알려 주세요 — always clarify which airport; in Seoul both are options and the routes differ significantly. From-to frame: 여기서 공항까지 어떻게 가요? — 서 (from here) + 까지 (to/until) makes the departure point explicit. Transport: 공항 버스 어디서 타요? / 공항 철도 어디서 타요? — 어디서 + 타다 (action verb) correctly uses 에서. Duration: 여기서 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요? is the natural follow-up once the route is established.

가르쳐 주세요 is the most common substitution error — 가르치다 is 'teach a subject/skill' and sounds as if you want a lesson, not directions. For giving information or directions, the correct verb is 알려 주다. Also, 공항 길 어디예요? ('where is the airport road?') is too literal; say 가는 길 알려 주세요 for route guidance.

mistakes: Saying 공항 가는 길 가르쳐 주세요 — 가르치다 means 'teach a subject', so it sounds like asking for a lesson. For directions use 알려 주다. 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and the favor verb: 공항 길 어디예요? is vague. To ask the route politely, use 알려 주세요. 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
Saying 공항 어떻게 가요 is fine for 'how', but to have them spell out the route, use 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.

english: Could you change my room, please?
usage: Polite — guest to front desk with a room problem
반말 — to a friend, not staff
방 좀 바꿔 주실 수 있어요?
Could you possibly change my room?
격식 / courteous — softer for a bigger request
Please move me to a different room.
examples: 옆방이 너무 시끄러워서요, 방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
The next room is too loud — could you change my room?
-서요 ending gives the reason politely before the request; this phrasing sounds considerate, not aggressive
A: 에어컨이 전혀 안 되는데, 다른 방으로 바꿔 주실 수 있어요? / B: 죄송합니다, 바로 확인해 드릴게요.
A: The air-con doesn't work at all — could you move me to another room? / B: I'm sorry about that, let me check right away.
Complete A/B: guest gives the problem, staff apologizes and acts — 다른 방으로 with 으로 (direction marker) is the correct particle
방 뷰가 주차장이에요. 혹시 바다 보이는 방으로 바꿔 주실 수 있어요?
My room overlooks a car park. Could you possibly switch me to a room with an ocean view?
Real situation: upgrade request framed politely — 혹시 ('by any chance') softens the ask when you're requesting something better
nuance: 방 좀 바꿔 주세요 asks hotel staff to move you to a different room; 바꾸다 is 'to swap/change', and -아/어 주세요 with 좀 frames it as a polite favor request rather than a complaint. Register is standard-polite; if the problem is significant (broken AC, loud neighbors), soften further to 바꿔 주실 수 있어요? or 바꿔 주시겠어요?. The nearby synonym 다른 방으로 옮겨 주세요 (옮기다 'to move/transfer') puts the emphasis on physically relocating you — both are correct, but 옮기다 sounds a touch more like a logistical move while 바꾸다 stresses the swap itself. Adding 으로 after the new room specification is essential: 다른 방으로 바꿔 주세요 (으로 = 'to/into'), not 다른 방을. The English-speaker error is using 변경하다 ('to formally modify/alter'), which fits changing a reservation date over the phone but sounds bureaucratically stiff when you're standing at the desk asking to be moved; in person, 바꾸다 is natural.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Please do the favor of swapping the room' — 바꾸다 is the everyday verb for swapping/changing something. The -아/어 주세요 favor pattern is what makes it a polite request. Specifying a destination requires 으로: 다른 방으로 바꿔 주세요 ('swap me to a different room').

Standard-polite 존댓말 with 좀. For a more serious problem (broken AC, safety issue) or a luxury hotel, upgrade to 바꿔 주실 수 있어요? or 바꿔 주시겠어요?. Adding the reason first (-서요 'because...') makes the request sound cooperative rather than demanding. 반말 바꿔 줘 is only for friends.

다른 방으로 옮겨 주세요 (옮기다 'to move/transfer') is nearly synonymous but emphasizes physical relocation — your bags move, not just the room number. 바꿔 주세요 emphasizes the swap of one room for another. In practice both are used; 옮기다 is slightly more common when you mention moving your belongings.

Reason-first pattern: 소음 때문에 방 좀 바꿔 주세요 / 에어컨이 고장 나서 방 좀 바꿔 주실 수 있어요? — stating the reason before the request with 때문에 or -서 makes you sound cooperative rather than demanding. Destination particle: 다른 방으로 바꿔 주세요 — 으로 is non-negotiable for the target room. Price: 같은 가격의 다른 방으로 바꿔 주실 수 있어요? — adding 같은 가격의 shows you're not asking for a free upgrade. Upgrade: 업그레이드 가능해요? or 더 좋은 방 있어요? are the natural ways to ask for a better room if you're willing to pay.

변경하다 ('to formally modify') sounds like filing a bureaucratic change request — too stiff for an in-person ask. Use 바꾸다 when speaking to staff at the desk. A second error is using 을 for the destination: 다른 방을 바꿔 주세요 is wrong; the destination always takes 으로 (다른 방으로 바꿔 주세요).

mistakes: Saying 방 변경해 주세요 — 변경하다 is formal 'modify' for bookings/schedules. To be moved rooms in person, use 바꾸다. 방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
Using 을 when naming the new room: 다른 방을 바꿔 주세요 is off. The destination takes 으로. 다른 방으로 바꿔 주세요.
방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and the favor verb, e.g. 방 바꿔! — that's blunt. Polite requests use 좀 ... 주세요. 방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
